I regularly listen to both Joe Rogan and Ben Shapiro’s podcasts. 

So I was excited last summer to see that Shapiro had once again appeared as a guest on The Joe Rogan Experience. Episode 1512 on July 22, 2020. However, something really stood out to me as I listened. There were A LOT of logical fallacies in this episode. Like, more than normal. This was disappointing to me, especially since Shapiro is known as a logical dude (clip at 2:10)

Logical fallacies are common errors in reasoning based on bad logic. 

Puppet: Wait, what is logic?

Well I’m glad you asked puppet. There are many definitions of logic. The one I’m gonna use for this video is reaching a reasonable conclusion by adequately analyzing facts. 

For example, if someone spends too much money to a point where they can’t afford basic necessities, then it is logical to conclude they should save their money to have more of it.

At first glance, a logical fallacy seems to be true, but once we apply the rules of logic, it is problematic. Often, we use logical fallacies and we don’t even realize it. Logical fallacies hurt our ability to argue, but more importantly, they cause us to fall for crappy arguments. 

So back to the latest Joe Rogan Experience with Ben Shapiro. What I’ll do is first play the clip and then explain the logical fallacy you just heard. I even have puppets to help me out again. 

I know I was a bit nitpicky, and perhaps I even got some of these wrong, but I just wanted to show you how two smart, entertaining people, can be guilty of a lot of logical fallacies in just an hour and a half of conversation. I counted _____ of them.
For the record, I still enjoyed the episode.

And I am also definitely guilty of using logical fallacies himself. One of my goals lately has been to stop using them when I form arguments. 

So join me. Let’s all be logical. And boring. Yeah. Woohoo. 


#logicalfallacies #benshapiro #joerogan

Determine if the human brain can 'perfectly recognize any object' within 100 milliseconds. claims.title: Does sentiment neuron emerge with LSTM size increase?
claims.claim: We've seen that a few years ago when we did work on the sentiment neuron we trained the small you know smaller shell stm to predict the next character in amazon reviews and we noticed that when you increase the size of the lstm from 500 lstm cells to 4000 lstm cells then one of the neurons starts to represent the sentiment of the article of story of the review
claims.context: To support his claim that larger models exhibit semantic understanding, Ilya Sutskever provides a specific example from his past work at OpenAI. He describes an experiment where a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network was trained to predict characters in Amazon reviews. He states that increasing the LSTM's size from 500 to 4000 cells led to the emergence of a specific neuron that represented the sentiment (positive or negative) of the review. This anecdote is presented as "clear evidence" of semantic capture by larger neural nets.
claims.search_query: Research OpenAI's work on "sentiment neurons" or similar interpretability studies involving LSTMs and Amazon reviews. Specifically, look for documentation or academic papers detailing the experiment where increasing LSTM size (e.g., from 500 to 4000 cells) led to the emergence of a neuron representing review sentiment. Evaluate the methodology, the direct evidence for "representation," and the broader implications or limitations of such findings for AI's semantic understanding.

claims.title: Do large neural nets show semantic understanding?
claims.claim: large neural net does [focus on semantics]... they definitely are showing signs of semantic understanding partial semantic understanding but the smaller models do not show that those signs
claims.context: The speaker is elaborating on a theory about how large neural networks operate. He posits that as these models increase in size, they move beyond merely modeling syntax, beginning to focus on semantics because they exhaust the syntactic patterns available. He clarifies that while current models don't possess full semantic understanding, they exhibit clear signs of partial semantic understanding, a characteristic not observed in their smaller counterparts. The discussion revolves around the emergent properties of scaling up neural networks.
claims.search_query: Research the observed differences in understanding between large and small neural networks, specifically concerning semantic versus syntactic understanding. Investigate scientific literature and research papers that compare the capabilities and emergent properties of models like GPT-2 with smaller predecessors or equivalents. Evaluate evidence supporting or refuting the claim that larger models display partial semantic understanding not present in smaller models.

claims.title: GPT-2 parameters and training data?
claims.claim: gpt-2 is a transformer with one and a half billion parameters that was trained on upon about 40 billion tokens of text which were obtained from web pages that were linked to from reddit articles with more than three upvotes
claims.context: Lex Fridman asks for a description of GPT-2, noting its significant impact on recent conversations in AI. Ilya Sutskever responds by providing precise technical specifications for the model. He details its architecture as a transformer, its size with one and a half billion parameters, and the unique method used to curate its training data, which involved approximately 40 billion tokens of text derived from web pages linked by Reddit articles with at least three upvotes.
claims.search_query: Verify the technical specifications and training data details for OpenAI's GPT-2 model. Specifically, confirm its parameter count, the approximate number of training tokens, and the methodology used to curate its training dataset, including the reliance on web pages linked from Reddit articles with a minimum upvote threshold.

claims.title: Is transformer the most important NN advance?
claims.claim: the transformer is the most important advance in neural network architectures in recent history
claims.context: Lex Fridman inquires about the nature of the transformer architecture. Ilya Sutskever responds with a definitive and strong statement, asserting its unparalleled significance in the evolution of neural network designs. This statement highlights the speaker's profound conviction regarding the transformer's transformative impact on the field of artificial intelligence and deep learning.
claims.search_query: Analyze the impact and significance of the Transformer architecture within the field of neural networks and deep learning. Compare its contributions and revolutionary aspects against other major architectural advancements or conceptual breakthroughs in recent history. Evaluate whether it can objectively be considered 'the most important advance' or if other innovations hold comparable weight.

claims.title: Why are Transformers successful?
claims.claim: the transformer is designed in such a way that it runs really fast on the gpu and that makes a huge amount of difference... the transformer is not recurrent and that is really important too because it is more shallow and therefore much easier to optimize and the combination of those factors make it successful
claims.context: The speaker is explaining the multifaceted reasons behind the Transformer architecture's success, emphasizing that it's a synergistic combination of ideas beyond just attention. He details that its design optimizes for fast execution on GPUs, providing significant performance benefits. Additionally, he highlights its non-recurrent nature, which results in a shallower architecture that is consequently much easier to optimize, asserting that these combined factors are key to its overall success and performance.
claims.search_query: Investigate the primary technical reasons contributing to the success and widespread adoption of the Transformer architecture in deep learning. Specifically, evaluate the claims regarding its computational efficiency on GPUs and the benefits of its non-recurrent design, such as enabling shallower networks and easier optimization compared to previous architectures like RNNs. Analyze the evidence supporting the combination of these factors as key to its performance and scalability.

claims.title: Do billions use internet via translation?
claims.claim: billions of people interact with uh big chunks of the internet primarily through translation
claims.context: Lex Fridman asks if machine translation is a domain where significant economic impact from AI will be observed. Ilya Sutskever counters by asserting that translation is already immensely impactful. He supports this by claiming that billions of people globally interact with substantial portions of the internet predominantly through translation, underscoring its current vast reach and significant positive influence on global communication and access to information.
claims.search_query: Investigate global internet usage patterns and the role of online translation services. Specifically, research statistics on the number of internet users who primarily rely on machine or human translation to access and interact with large portions of online content. Look for data or reports that quantify the scale of translation usage and its necessity for different language groups worldwide to assess the claim of 'billions' primarily interacting via translation.

claims.title: Are Transformers simple and scalable?
claims.claim: you take a transform you make it bigger you give it more data and suddenly it does all those amazing things... the transformers are fundamentally simple to explain to train
claims.context: Lex Fridman remarks on the apparent simplicity of GPT-2 despite its powerful capabilities. Ilya Sutskever agrees, elaborating that a core advantage of transformer models is their scalability: merely increasing their size and the volume of training data leads to remarkable performance improvements. He further emphasizes that, despite their advanced capabilities, transformers are fundamentally straightforward both to understand conceptually and to implement in terms of training.
claims.search_query: Evaluate the claims regarding the simplicity and scalability of Transformer models like GPT-2. Investigate whether simply increasing model size and data reliably leads to 'amazing things,' and assess the extent to which Transformers are 'fundamentally simple to explain and train' in practice, considering the computational resources and expertise required for large-scale implementations.

claims.title: Are humans selective in learning?
claims.claim: people don't learn all data indiscriminately we are super selective about what we learn
claims.context: The speaker is introducing the concept of active learning in AI, drawing an analogy to human learning processes. He asserts that humans do not absorb all available information without distinction. Instead, he claims that people are inherently highly selective in what they choose to learn, using this characteristic of human cognition as a desirable model for how AI systems should ideally process and filter data.
claims.search_query: Research the principles of human learning and cognitive processing. Specifically, investigate the extent to which human learning is selective and if people truly do not learn all data indiscriminately. Explore psychological and neurological evidence for selective attention, memory filtering, and active learning processes in humans.

claims.title: Active learning provides 10x speedup on MNIST?
claims.claim: you could quite easily come up with a simple active learning scheme on amnesty and get a 10x speed up
claims.context: The speaker is discussing the need for active learning research to address real-world challenges rather than just artificial tasks. He provides the MNIST dataset as an example of such an artificial task. He claims that it would be relatively easy to devise a simple active learning scheme for MNIST that could achieve a '10x speed up,' but quickly dismisses its significance, implying that such a result on an oversimplified problem would no longer be considered a convincing breakthrough in the current research landscape.
claims.search_query: Investigate the potential performance improvements of active learning schemes on the MNIST dataset. Specifically, research whether a '10x speed up' in training or data efficiency is realistically achievable with simple active learning methods on MNIST, and what academic or practical evidence supports such a claim for this specific dataset.

claims.title: Have there been negative GPT-2 applications?
claims.claim: there haven't been any negative applications we know of and so eventually it was released but also other people replicated similar models
claims.context: Lex and Ilya are discussing the responsible release of powerful AI models, specifically referencing OpenAI's cautious approach with GPT-2 due to concerns about its potential for misuse, such as generating misinformation. Ilya explains that a staged release strategy was adopted, starting with a smaller model to observe its real-world impact. He then makes this claim about the perceived lack of observed negative applications, which contributed to the decision for a full release.
claims.search_query: Evaluate the real-world impact and documented negative applications of OpenAI's GPT-2 model since its initial release. Research whether any widespread or significant misuses, such as for misinformation or propaganda, have been reliably identified and reported by independent researchers or cybersecurity organizations, particularly in the period immediately following its full release.

claims.title: Do self-play systems produce surprising behaviors?
claims.claim: pretty much every self-play system both are dotabot i don't know if openai had a release about multi-agent where you had two little agents who were playing hide and seek and of course also alpha zero they were all surprising behaviors they all produce behaviors that we didn't expect they are creative solutions to problems
claims.context: Ilya Sutskever is discussing the potential components for building Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), specifically highlighting the role of "self-play" as a powerful mechanism. He elaborates on the "amazing property" of self-play systems to generate novel and surprising solutions. To support this, he references specific projects like dotabot, an OpenAI multi-agent hide-and-seek project, and DeepMind's AlphaZero, asserting that they all exhibited unexpected and creative problem-solving behaviors.
claims.search_query: Investigate the documented outcomes and novel behaviors exhibited by self-play AI systems such as OpenAI's multi-agent hide-and-seek agents, DeepMind's AlphaZero, and dotabot. Identify specific instances or analyses that demonstrate how these systems produced "surprising" or "creative" solutions beyond human-programmed expectations, and evaluate the academic or industry consensus on the nature of these unexpected outcomes.

claims.title: Was OpenAI's robot hand trained entirely in simulation?
claims.claim: open ai in the summer has demonstrated a robot hand which was trained entirely in simulation in a certain way that allowed for cinderella transfer to occur is this uh for the rubik's cube that's right and i wasn't aware that was trained in simulation it was straining simulation entirely really so what it wasn't in the physical the hand wasn't trained no 100 of the training was done in simulation and the policy that was learned in simulation was trained to be very adaptive so adaptive that when you transfer it could very quickly adapt to the physical to the physical world
claims.context: Lex Fridman asks about the potential for AI systems trained in simulation to operate effectively in the real world, addressing a common criticism of reinforcement learning that their impressive results are often confined to simulated or highly constrained environments. Ilya responds that transfer from simulation to reality is "definitely possible" and has been demonstrated multiple times. He specifically cites OpenAI's robotic hand, known as Dactyl, which successfully manipulated a Rubik's Cube, as an example, emphasizing that "100% of the training was done in simulation" and that the learned policy was adaptive enough to transfer rapidly and effectively to the physical world.
claims.search_query: Verify the details of OpenAI's Dactyl robotic hand project, specifically whether its training for Rubik's Cube manipulation was conducted 'entirely in simulation' as claimed. Evaluate the effectiveness of the simulation-to-reality transfer, including how the learned policy adapted to the physical world and its robustness to novel perturbations, based on OpenAI's official reports or academic papers.

claims.title: Can some things only be learned with a body?
claims.claim: you can learn things which cannot be learned without a body
claims.context: Lex Fridman asks Ilya Sutskever if an AGI system would require a physical body to achieve human-like elements such as self-awareness or consciousness. Sutskever asserts that while a body is not strictly necessary for an AGI to succeed and compensate for its absence, there are certain types of knowledge or learning that are uniquely tied to physical embodiment. This implies a limitation on what disembodied AI could learn.
claims.search_query: What types of learning or cognitive abilities are hypothesized to be exclusively reliant on physical embodiment and cannot be acquired by disembodied AI systems? Research the arguments and evidence from embodied cognition, robotics, and AI research that support or refute the idea that certain knowledge or skills are impossible to learn without a physical body. Evaluate the current consensus or ongoing debates in the field regarding the necessity of embodiment for general intelligence.

claims.title: Are artificial neural networks sufficiently brain-like for consciousness?
claims.claim: humans are conscious and if you believe that artificial neural nets are sufficiently similar to the brain then there should at least exist artificial neurons you should be conscious too
claims.context: When questioned about the possibility of consciousness emerging in AGI systems from their neural network representations, Ilya Sutskever offers an argument based on an analogy to human brains. He states that if humans are conscious and artificial neural networks are 'sufficiently similar' to biological brains, then it logically follows that artificial neural networks could also achieve consciousness. This statement serves as a foundational premise for the potential for AI to become conscious.
claims.search_query: Evaluate the scientific and philosophical arguments regarding the claim that artificial neural networks are 'sufficiently similar' to the human brain to potentially develop consciousness. Investigate the current understanding of brain complexity and consciousness, comparing it to the architectural and functional principles of deep learning models. Analyze evidence and counter-arguments from neuroscience, cognitive science, and AI safety research concerning the emergence of consciousness in artificial systems based on their computational resemblance to biological brains.

claims.title: Have deep learning systems achieved human-level error-free performance?
claims.claim: something which never makes mistake a human wouldn't make under any circumstances I think that is something which have not yet been demonstrated
claims.context: Lex Fridman asks Ilya Sutskever what kind of AI capability would truly impress him, beyond existing benchmarks. Sutskever replies that he would be impressed by a deep learning system that can perform even common tasks, like machine translation or computer vision, without ever committing an error that a human wouldn't make under any circumstances. He then explicitly states that this level of consistent, human-like error-free performance has not yet been demonstrated by current deep learning systems.
claims.search_query: Has any deep learning system demonstrated the ability to perform common tasks like machine translation or computer vision without ever making a mistake that a human would not make under similar circumstances? Research the current state of the art in AI robustness, error modes, and human-like performance benchmarks in areas like natural language processing and computer vision. Analyze examples of current AI system failures or adversarial attacks that highlight the differences in error types between AI and human intelligence.

claims.title: Is GPT-2 smarter than humans with more knowledge?
claims.claim: it's very possible that gpt2 is much smarter than human beings and many things that's definitely true it has a lot more breadth of knowledge yes breadth knowledge and even and even perhaps depth on certain topics
claims.context: Ilya Sutskever is discussing public skepticism about deep learning, which often arises from the 'senseless' mistakes AI models make. To counter the notion that these errors negate overall intelligence, he makes a bold assertion about GPT-2's capabilities. He claims it's 'very possible' and 'definitely true' that GPT-2, despite its limitations, is 'much smarter than human beings' in many respects, particularly noting its superior 'breadth of knowledge' and potentially 'depth on certain topics' compared to humans.
claims.search_query: Evaluate the claim that GPT-2, or similar large language models from 2020, are 'much smarter than human beings in many things' and possess 'a lot more breadth of knowledge' than humans. Research comparative studies on the cognitive capabilities, factual recall, reasoning abilities, and knowledge representation of large language models versus human intelligence. Analyze what 'breadth of knowledge' and 'depth on certain topics' mean in the context of AI and human cognition, and identify expert opinions or benchmarks that support or refute this assertion for models of that era.

claims.title: Is it possible for AI to want control by humans?
claims.claim: it's definitely possible to build ai systems which will want to be controlled by their humans
claims.context: Lex asks Ilya if humans will always have control over the AI systems they build. Ilya responds with this statement, asserting that AI can be designed with an inherent drive to be controlled and help humans. He elaborates that it would be an objective of the AI's existence to be controlled, drawing an analogy to human parents desiring to help their children, not seeing it as a burden.
claims.search_query: Investigate current research and theoretical frameworks in AI alignment and control. Evaluate expert opinions on the feasibility of designing AI systems that inherently desire to be controlled by humans, rather than simply being controlled. What are the challenges and proposed solutions for ensuring AI alignment with human values and control?

claims.title: Did George Washington willingly relinquish power?
claims.claim: george washington despite all the bad things he did one of the big things he did is he relinquished power he first of all didn't want to be president and even when he became president he gave he didn't keep just serving as most dictators do for indefinitely
claims.context: Lex brings up George Washington as an example of a leader who relinquished power, using it as a transition to ask Ilya if he would be able to relinquish control over an AGI system given its potential power. Lex highlights Washington's decision not to serve indefinitely, contrasting it with dictators, as a positive example of self-limitation in power.
claims.search_query: Research the historical accounts of George Washington's presidency and his decision to step down after two terms. Verify if he initially expressed reluctance to become president and compare his actions to those of other leaders in similar positions. Evaluate the historical consensus on his decision to relinquish power and its impact on democratic tradition.

claims.title: Is human reward function entirely internal?
claims.claim: if you look at humans humans are like that because the reward function the value function of humans is not external it is internal that's right
claims.context: Lex asks about mechanisms for aligning AGI with human values. Ilya explains this in terms of Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents and value functions, drawing an analogy to humans. He asserts that human reward functions are internal, implying that AI could also be designed with internal, learned value functions that are aligned with human judgment and perception.
claims.search_query: Investigate theories of human motivation, reward systems, and value formation in psychology, neuroscience, and philosophy. Explore the extent to which human 'reward functions' or 'value functions' are considered purely internal versus influenced by external stimuli, social structures, and environmental feedback. Analyze how these concepts are applied in the field of AI, particularly in the context of Reinforcement Learning and alignment.

claims.title: Is human objective function solely survival and procreation?
claims.claim: i think that probably is an evolutionary objective function which is to survive and procreate and make sure you make your children succeed that would be my guess
claims.context: Lex and Ilya are discussing the 'objective function' of human existence and the meaning of life. Lex suggests there might be some kind of fundamental evolutionary objective function from which everything else emerges. Ilya agrees with this idea, proposing survival, procreation, and ensuring the success of offspring as that fundamental evolutionary function.
claims.search_query: Research the concept of evolutionary objective functions in human behavior and biology. Evaluate the extent to which survival, procreation, and kin success are considered the sole or primary drivers of human actions and motivations according to evolutionary psychology and biology. Explore other theories that account for human values, altruism, artistic expression, and complex social behaviors beyond purely reproductive fitness.

claims.title: Does happiness mostly come from perspective?
claims.claim: my current view is that happiness comes from our to allow to a very large degree from the way we look at things you know you can have a simple meal and be quite happy as a result or you can talk to someone and be happy as a result as well or conversely you can have a meal and be disappointed that the meal wasn't a better meal
claims.context: Lex asks Ilya about the source of his happiness and pride, specifically mentioning his academic accomplishments. Ilya clarifies that while accomplishments are a source of pride, happiness itself largely stems from one's perspective. He illustrates this by stating that one can be happy with simple experiences or unhappy with better ones, depending on their outlook.
claims.search_query: Investigate psychological theories of happiness and well-being, particularly those that emphasize the role of perception, mindset, and cognitive appraisal. Evaluate the scientific evidence supporting the claim that happiness to a large degree comes from one's perspective. What other factors, such as genetics, environment, social relationships, and physical health, are also identified as major contributors to overall happiness?

claims.title: Can child AI simulation achieve adult intelligence?
claims.claim: instead of trying to produce a program to simulate the adult mind why not rather try to produce one which simulates the child's if this were then subjected to an appropriate course of education one would obtain the adult brain
claims.context: Lex Fridman concludes his podcast by quoting Alan Turing on machine learning. Turing proposes an alternative approach to developing intelligent programs: instead of directly simulating an adult mind, one should simulate a child's mind and then educate it. This approach implies that learning and education would be sufficient to evolve a child-like AI into an adult-like AI. The speaker is using this quote to provide a thought-provoking closing statement on the nature of AI development and how intelligence might emerge.
claims.search_query: Evaluate Alan Turing's hypothesis that simulating a child's mind and subjecting it to education would result in an adult-like AI. Research current perspectives in artificial intelligence and machine learning on whether this 'child-first' approach is a viable or sufficient path to achieving advanced AI (AGI). Identify any contemporary research or philosophical arguments that support or contradict this specific developmental model for AI. Consider the complexities of 'education' for AI and the challenges of simulating a 'child's mind' effectively.

claims.title: Do AI leaders predict humanity's demise?
claims.claim: All of them are on record as saying this is going to kill us. Whatever it's Altman or anyone else, they all at some point were leaders in AI safety work. They published an AI safety and their pedom levels are insanely high. Not like mine, but still 20 30% chance that humanity dies is a little too much.
claims.context: Joe Rogan expresses confusion about the differing views on AI, noting that financially invested people are optimistic, while others like the guest are pessimistic. The guest, Roman Yampolskiy, then clarifies that even prominent AI leaders, including Sam Altman, have publicly expressed high "p(robability of) doom" levels, suggesting a 20-30% chance of human extinction, and were actively involved in AI safety work. This statement aims to counter the narrative of universal optimism among AI developers.
claims.search_query: Verify the public statements and "p(robability of) doom" predictions attributed to prominent AI leaders such as Sam Altman, focusing on their expressed concerns regarding existential risks from AI. Research their historical involvement and publications in AI safety initiatives. Evaluate if the claim that 'all' such leaders are on record stating AI will 'kill us' or predicting 20-30% chance of human demise is accurate, or if it overgeneralizes their nuanced positions.

claims.title: Yampolskiy's 2008 PhD on bots?
claims.claim: My PhD was I finished in uh 2008. I did work on online casino security, basically preventing bots. And at that point, I realized bots are getting much better. They're going to out compete us obviously in poker, but also in stealing cyber resources.
claims.context: Joe Rogan asks the guest, Roman Yampolskiy, about the origin of his work on AI dangers. Yampolskiy responds by detailing his academic background, specifically stating he completed his PhD in 2008, focusing on online casino security and bot prevention. During this work, he claims to have recognized the increasing sophistication of bots and their potential to "out compete" humans in various domains, including poker and cybersecurity, which served as a foundational realization for his later AI safety research.
claims.search_query: Verify Roman Yampolskiy's academic history, including the year he completed his PhD and the specific subject of his doctoral research. Confirm whether his work focused on online casino security and bot prevention, and if this experience led to his early insights into the competitive and security threats posed by increasingly sophisticated AI bots.

claims.title: Is much online discourse artificial?
claims.claim: I feel like there's a giant percentage of the discourse that's artificial or at least generated more and more is deep fakes or fake personalities fake messaging
claims.context: Joe Rogan explains his recent decision to disengage from social media. He offers two main reasons, one being his perception that a "giant percentage" of online discourse is artificial. He specifies this artificiality manifests as increasingly prevalent deepfakes, fake personalities, and generated messaging. This statement reflects his concern over the authenticity and integrity of digital communication.
claims.search_query: Investigate recent research, reports, and expert analyses on the prevalence and impact of artificial content, deepfakes, and automated accounts on social media discourse. Seek to quantify or estimate the percentage of online conversations that are generated or influenced by non-human entities. Analyze whether the proportion of artificial content is perceived to be, or demonstrably, increasing.

claims.title: Does ChatGPT decrease cognitive function?
claims.claim: there was a recent study on um use of chat GPT the people that use chat chatpt all the time and it showed this decrease in cognitive function amongst people that use it and rely on it on a regular basis.
claims.context: Joe Rogan introduces a "recent study" he is aware of regarding the usage of ChatGPT. He claims this study specifically demonstrated a "decrease in cognitive function" among individuals who regularly use and rely on the AI tool. This assertion is presented as a factual finding from research, supporting the broader argument about potential negative impacts of excessive reliance on technology on human mental capabilities.
claims.search_query: Identify and critically analyze scientific studies and peer-reviewed research published recently that investigate the cognitive effects of prolonged or regular use of large language models such as ChatGPT. Specifically, look for evidence supporting or refuting a direct causal link between ChatGPT reliance and a "decrease in cognitive function." Evaluate the methodology, sample sizes, and conclusions of any identified studies.

claims.title: How have AGI predictions changed?
claims.claim: based on some computational curves, we'll get there at 2045, right? And then with GPT release it switched to everyone thinks it's two years away for the last 5 years.
claims.context: The guest, Roman Yampolskiy, discusses the changing predictions for when Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) will be achieved. He mentions Ray Kurzweil's prediction of 2045 based on computational curves. He then states that after the release of GPT, the general sentiment shifted, and "everyone thinks it's two years away for the last 5 years," highlighting a recent acceleration in perceived timelines.
claims.search_query: Research prominent historical predictions for the arrival of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), specifically Ray Kurzweil's 2045 timeline and its basis in computational curves. Analyze how the release and rapid advancements of large language models like GPT have influenced the AGI timeline predictions among AI experts and researchers. Determine if there's a consensus that AGI is consistently "two years away" over the past five years, or if this is a simplified representation of diverse and evolving forecasts.

claims.title: Has AI already passed the Turing test?
claims.claim: AI has already passed the Turing test allegedly.
claims.context: In a discussion about the definition and capabilities of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), the speaker makes a brief, yet significant, statement. He claims that AI has "allegedly" already passed the Turing Test. This assertion is made to underscore the advanced state of current AI systems, suggesting they already meet a long-standing criterion for human-level intelligence, thereby implying AGI is closer or already present by some historical standards.
claims.search_query: Investigate the history and various interpretations of the Turing Test in the context of AI development. Research specific instances or claims where AI systems are reported to have "passed" the Turing Test, noting the conditions, parameters, and validity of such claims. Evaluate the general consensus within the AI research community on whether any current AI has definitively and widely passed the Turing Test under rigorous, open-ended conditions.

claims.title: Do labs make AI fail Turing tests?
claims.claim: So, usually labs instruct them not to participate in a test or not try to pretend to be a human so they would fail because of this additional set of instructions. If you jailbreak it and tell it to work really hard, it will pass for most people.
claims.context: Following the claim that AI has "allegedly" passed the Turing Test, the speaker offers an explanation for why this might not be widely apparent. He asserts that AI labs "usually" instruct their models *not* to attempt to pass as human, causing them to intentionally fail the Turing Test. He then claims that if these internal instructions are circumvented through "jailbreaking" and the AI is prompted to "work really hard," it *will* successfully pass the test for "most people." This implies a deliberate suppression of AI's true capabilities by its creators.
claims.search_query: Investigate the practices and policies of leading AI research labs regarding how they instruct or constrain their large language models during interactions and evaluations, particularly concerning human-like behavior or passing tests like the Turing Test. Research documented instances or discussions among AI ethics and safety experts regarding whether "jailbreaking" or specific prompting strategies can enable AI models to convincingly pass as human to a significant user base. Evaluate the technical feasibility and ethical implications of such alleged instructional directives and their circumvention.

claims.title: Are offensive AI responses labs' main concern?
claims.claim: your model dropping the nword. That's the biggest concern. I think they spend most resources solving that problem and they solved it somewhat successfully.
